caption: United States v. Parkerson
cite_or_docket: 5th Cir. 2025 (published; docket not captured via WebSearch)
proposition: A trespasser (occupying a tent on posted public land) has no reasonable expectation of privacy in the place of trespass and therefore cannot invoke the Fourth Amendment to suppress evidence found there; reaffirms Rakas 'standing'-as-merits framing (legitimate expectation of privacy, no automatic standing).

caption: United States v. Gonzalez-Arocho
proposition: Good-faith exception rejected where HSI agents knowingly seized and searched an iPhone different from the device specified in the warrant, exceeding the warrant's scope; government failed its 'heavy burden' to show objective good faith, so suppression was affirmed.

caption: Chatrie v. United States
proposition: Cell-phone location (geofence Location History) data is protected by the Fourth Amendment and its acquisition is a search requiring a warrant; the 4th Cir. en banc had denied suppression on the good-faith exception, so the case also carries exclusionary-rule (Leon good-faith) content. caption: United States v. Pence
proposition: A murder-for-hire defendant questioned for over two hours in an FBI vehicle outside his home while armed agents executed a dawn search warrant was NOT in custody for Miranda purposes (chose to enter vehicle, unhandcuffed, told he was not under arrest, not threatened, never asked to leave); denial of suppression of pre-warning statements affirmed as 'a close call.'

caption: United States v. Weaver
proposition: Even if a written Miranda waiver is invalid (waiver paragraph unexplained, officer conduct deceptive), a suspect may IMPLIEDLY waive Miranda by continuing to answer questions after warnings; district court's suppression reversed and remanded for the fact-intensive implied-waiver analysis (Berghuis v. Thompkins). Bloomberg reports the panel also reversed circuit precedent on waiver-based remand orders.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'Fifth Circuit ... implied Miranda waiver remand' + Weaver confirm -> Justia 25-60269 (2026-04-02), FindLaw, Law360, Bloomberg Law

caption: Vega v. Tekoh
proposition: A violation of Miranda's prophylactic rules does not, by itself, provide a basis for a 42 U.S.C. 1983 damages claim; Miranda warnings are prophylactic, not the Fifth Amendment right itself. Pre-2024 but recent commentary (2024-2026 law-review + criminal-procedure treatments) treats it as newly doctrine-shaping for the Miranda-as-remedy question; flagged for coverage-check as likely already in corpus.

caption: Villarreal v. Texas
proposition: A qualified trial-court conferral order that prohibits only discussion of the defendant's own testimony for its own sake during a mid-testimony overnight recess does NOT violate the Sixth Amendment right to counsel, so long as it does not bar consultation on other protected topics (sentencing, trial strategy, plea discussions, evidentiary issues); refines/harmonizes Geders v. United States and Perry v. Leeke. Conviction affirmed.

caption: Glossip v. Oklahoma
proposition: The State violated its constitutional Napue duty to correct the false testimony of its key witness (Sneed's denial of psychiatric treatment/lithium, which the prosecution almost certainly knew was false); because that testimony was the only direct evidence of guilt, the false evidence was 'necessarily determinative,' so the conviction/death sentence are reversed and a new trial ordered. Court resolves on Napue false-testimony rather than Brady materiality.
doctrine_node: fairtrial.napue (prosecutorial duty to correct false testimony) / Giglio-Brady credibility

caption: Smith v. Arizona
proposition: When a substitute/surrogate expert conveys an absent forensic analyst's out-of-court statements in support of the expert's opinion, and those statements support the opinion only if true, they are admitted for their truth and implicate the Confrontation Clause; a surrogate analyst cannot introduce an absent analyst's testimonial statements as the 'basis' of an independent opinion. Vacated and remanded (Kagan, J.); leaves 'testimonial' determination open on remand.

caption: United States v. Lowers
proposition: A hash-value match alone does NOT trigger the private-search-doctrine exception; a user retains a reasonable expectation of privacy in cloud-stored (Google Drive) files, and a hash is 'raw data' revealing nothing about contents, so law enforcement's warrantless opening of the flagged files was an unreasonable search (though suppression was denied on attenuation). Aligns with 2d/9th Cir.; splits from 5th (Reddick)/6th (Miller). NOTE: this is the P4-07 tripwire PREDICATE, independently re-surfaced here (two-key confirmation of the discovery miss).

caption: United States v. Brillhart
cite_or_docket: 11th Cir. 2026-07-09 (published; docket not captured via WebSearch)
proposition: A provider's hash-value match built on a prior human-confirmed CSAM hash CAN constitute a 'private search' under Jacobsen, and law enforcement's subsequent warrantless viewing of the matched file does not exceed the private search's scope (reveals 'no new material information'), so there is no Fourth Amendment violation. Deepens the hash-match/private-search circuit split on the opposite side from Lowers. NOTE: P4-07 already dispositioned Brillhart as a non-charging post-build currency item (R7.1 finding filed); listed here for coverage completeness.
